extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, applicants, DHS/USCIS analysts, policy analysts, and stakeholders participating in rulemaking/notice-and-comment
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and procedural guidance in DHS's Final Rule on the public charge ground of inadmissibility, including what factors are considered in determinations, which benefits are excluded, population and baseline definitions, and the cost‑benefit and paperwork burden assumptions used to quantify impacts (forms, fees, time burdens, rates, and discounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors for public charge determination
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge, immigration officers must, at a minimum, consider certain factors, namely the noncitizen's age; health; and family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five factors are the statutorily specified baseline for public charge determinations. DHS's analysis and information collection (e.g., Form I-485 changes) are designed to collect information related to these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of affidavits of support (section 213A)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider any affidavit of support submitted under section 213A of the INA (8 U.S.C. 1183a) on behalf of the applicant when determining whether the applicant may become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sponsor executes an Affidavit of Support under section 213A they establish a legally enforceable contract with an obligation to financially support the applicant and reimburse benefit granting agencies. For most family-based and some employment-based immigrants, a sufficient affidavit of support is required; failure to meet the requirement results in inadmissibility on public charge grounds without review of the statutory factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from public charge inadmissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There are statutory and regulatory classes of applicants for admission, adjustment of status, or registry that are exempt from inadmissibility based on the public charge ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS removes individuals in exempt categories from the population subject to public charge review when estimating affected populations; tables in the preamble list the exempt classes. Exemptions and waivers affect who must be reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits excluded from consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider the receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c), such as SNAP or other nutrition programs, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicaid (other than for long‑term use of institutional services under section 1905(a) of the Social Security Act), housing benefits, any benefits related to immunizations or testing for communicable diseases, or other supplemental or special‑purpose benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification is intended to reduce uncertainty and confusion for applicants and decisionmakers by identifying explicitly which benefits are out of scope for public charge consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not consider benefits received by dependents
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS states a bright‑line rule against considering the receipt of public benefits by an applicant's dependents (such as a U.S. citizen child in a mixed‑status household).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant will not be penalized in the public charge determination for benefits accessed by household members or dependents; this bright‑line rule is a substantive limitation on relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary dependence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary dependence connotes significant reliance on the government for support and means something more than dependence that is merely transient or supplementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS clarifies that only substantial, non‑transitory reliance on public assistance should be construed as primary dependence in public charge assessments; this informs adjudicator weighing of benefit receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disability and long‑term institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule clarifies DHS's approach to consideration of disability and long‑term institutionalization at government expense in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains how these conditions are evaluated under the statutory factors (e.g., health and potential need for government‑funded institutional services) and notes the limited circumstances (e.g., Medicaid long‑term institutional services) that bear on the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Form I-485 to collect public‑charge relevant information
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule changes the Form I‑485 to collect additional information relevant to the public charge inadmissibility determination (including additional instructions and questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form redesign moves some previously open‑ended narrative questions to multiple‑choice to reduce time; however, the additional questions will increase the time burden per applicant (estimated +0.75 hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS public charge bonds: acceptance, form, amount, cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS added streamlined provisions to clarify acceptance, form, and amount of USCIS public charge bonds, as well as cancellation of public charge bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural clarifications govern when bonds are appropriate and how they are handled administratively; the preamble indicates these are codified to reduce uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baselines for cost‑benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS compares the final rule's impacts relative to two baselines: the No Action Baseline (implementation consistent with the 1999 Interim Field Guidance) and the Pre‑Guidance Baseline (a trajectory before the 1999 Interim Field Guidance existed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables and quantified estimates present impacts relative to each baseline. The choice of baseline affects estimated net costs and benefits and is explained in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population projection method for affected applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS projects the affected population for the 10‑year period beginning FY 2022 based on historical Form I‑485 receipts from FY 2014–FY 2018 and uses the 5‑year average to estimate the annual population subject to public charge review (estimated annual average 501,520).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS excludes FY 2019–FY 2021 from projections due to potential data anomalies and acknowledges this method may undercount applicants at ports of entry; limitations and uncertainty are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity cost valuation for applicants' time
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS uses the effective minimum wage plus weighted average benefits of $17.11 per hour ($11.80 effective minimum wage + $5.31 average benefits) as a proxy for the opportunity cost of time for individuals applying for adjustment of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS justifies this proxy because a large share of applicants are family‑based and may earn near the minimum; it notes commenters suggested alternative rates but provided no usable data. The benefits‑to‑wage multiplier used is 1.45 based on BLS employer cost data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor time valuation assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: For opportunity cost estimates of sponsors completing affidavits of support, DHS uses $39.55 per hour as the total compensation (wages + benefits) based on BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses a higher wage assumption for sponsors because it expects sponsors to have adequate means and likely be employed; this rate is applied to time burdens for Form I‑864 and related forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time burden estimates per form and component
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS provides specific time burdens used in calculations: Form I‑485 baseline 6.42 hours per response (increased by 0.75 hours to 7.17 in final rule); biometrics total time 3.67 hours; Form I‑693 2.5 hours; Form I‑912 1.17 hours; Form I‑864 6 hours; Form I‑864A 1.75 hours; Form I‑864EZ 2.5 hours; Form I‑864W 1 hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time burdens include reviewing instructions, gathering documents, completing forms, preparing statements, attending biometrics/civil surgeon appointments, waiting time, and submitting materials. DHS uses these hours to compute opportunity cost of time for applicants and sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary fee and cost assumptions used
rubrics_metrics.description: Key fee/cost assumptions used in the analysis include: Form I‑485 filing fee $1,140; biometrics services fee $85; medical exam average cost $493.75 (range $20–$1,000 depending on civil surgeon and required vaccinations/tests); estimated average roundtrip to ASC 50 miles; GSA mileage rate $0.585/mile yielding $29.25 travel cost per biometrics trip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS aggregates these fees with opportunity costs to estimate total current annual costs (e.g., total current annual cost for filing Form I‑485 estimated at $715,613,873). Variability in medical exam fees is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption each applicant travels independently to ASC
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS assumes each applicant will travel independently to an Application Support Center (ASC) to submit biometrics, imposing a travel cost on each applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption feeds into per‑applicant travel cost estimates (50‑mile roundtrip and GSA rate) and thus influences aggregate travel cost totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of baseline costs versus new regulatory costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs described as baseline include current costs associated with completing and filing Form I‑485 (e.g., biometrics, medical exam, affidavits of support, fee waivers). The final rule's new quantified costs are primarily the additional 0.75 hours to complete Form I‑485 for applicants subject to public charge review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS distinguishes between costs already incurred under the baseline and incremental costs attributable to the rule; only incremental costs are counted as new regulatory costs in the comparison to the No Action Baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discounting for 10‑year cost totals
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS reports undiscounted 10‑year totals and discounted 10‑year totals using 3‑percent and 7‑percent discount rates (e.g., ten‑year discounted net costs ~$54,767,280 at 3% and ~$45,094,175 at 7%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with OMB guidance, DHS presents both discount rates to show present value sensitivity to discounting assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified cost and savings categories (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS quantifies new annual direct costs from increased time to complete Form I‑485 (~$6,435,755 annually) and identifies specific savings (e.g., T nonimmigrants applying for adjustment of status will no longer need to submit Form I‑601, producing estimated annual savings of ~$15,359 for that group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis aggregates fees, opportunity costs, biometrics fees, travel, medical exam costs, and sponsor time costs to compute total current annual costs and net incremental costs of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of data limitations and unquantified impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges limitations in available data (e.g., inability to quantify CBP costs or the number of noncitizens who might be deemed inadmissible at ports of entry) and notes that such limitations could understate total costs/benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where DHS cannot quantify impacts, it qualitatively acknowledges potential effects. The population estimates intentionally exclude certain applicant groups due to data limitations and potential underestimation risk is stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of historical years for projections
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS selects FY 2014–FY 2018 as the historical period to project future Form I‑485 application counts because FY 2019–FY 2021 may include data anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this fixed historical window and 5‑year averages produces the projected annual filing population used in cost estimates; DHS explains rationale and limitations of this choice in the preamble.
